subject: English
q: The following sentence contains a modifier error: “Walking down the street, the trees were swaying in the wind.” Choose the correct version.
o: The trees, walking down the street, were swaying in the wind.
Walking down the street, the swaying of the trees was noticed.
Walking down the street, the trees were swaying in the wind.
Walking down the street, I noticed the trees swaying in the wind.
explanation: The participle “walking down the street” must refer to a person who can walk, so “I” must be the subject of the main clause.

subject: English
q: Which sentence corrects the modifier error in: “Looking out of the aircraft window, the mountains appeared covered in snow.”?
o: Looking out of the aircraft window, the mountains appeared covered in snow.
Looking out of the aircraft window, we saw that the mountains were covered in snow.
Looking out of the aircraft window, snow covered the mountains.
The mountains, looking out of the aircraft window, appeared covered in snow.
explanation: Only people can look out of a window, so the main clause must begin with the people doing it (“we”).

subject: English
q: Choose the sentence that fixes the misplaced or dangling phrase in: “Having been repaired, I drove the car back to Lahore.”
o: Having been repaired, I drove the car back to Lahore.
Having been repaired, back to Lahore I drove the car.
Having been repaired, the car was driven back to Lahore.
I, having been repaired, drove the car back to Lahore.
explanation: It was the car, not the speaker, that had been repaired, so “the car” must be the subject after the phrase.

subject: English
q: The following sentence contains a modifier error: “Arriving late, the meeting had already started.” Choose the correct version.
o: Arriving late, I found that the meeting had already started.
The meeting, arriving late, had already started.
Arriving late, the meeting had already started.
Arriving late, the start of the meeting had already happened.
explanation: A meeting cannot arrive; the participle needs a human subject such as “I”.

subject: English
q: Which sentence corrects the modifier error in: “While cooking dinner, the smoke alarm went off.”?
o: While cooking dinner, the smoke alarm went off.
While cooking dinner, off went the smoke alarm.
While I was cooking dinner, the smoke alarm went off.
The smoke alarm went off while cooking dinner.
explanation: The alarm was not cooking; giving the “while” clause its own subject removes the dangling modifier.

subject: English
q: Choose the sentence that fixes the misplaced or dangling phrase in: “To pass the examination, hard work is necessary.”
o: To pass the examination, hard work is necessary.
Hard work, to pass the examination, is necessary.
To pass the examination, working hard is necessary.
To pass the examination, you must work hard.
explanation: An introductory infinitive needs a doer in the main clause; “you” is the person who must pass.

subject: English
q: The following sentence contains a modifier error: “After finishing the report, the lights in the office were switched off.” Choose the correct version.
o: After finishing the report, the lights in the office were switched off.
After finishing the report, the officer switched off the lights in the office.
The lights in the office, after finishing the report, were switched off.
After finishing the report, the switching off of the lights took place.
explanation: The phrase “after finishing the report” needs a subject who finished it, here “the officer”.

subject: English
q: Which sentence corrects the modifier error in: “When only a child, my grandfather taught me to read the Quran.”?
o: When I was only a child, my grandfather taught me to read the Quran.
When only a child, the Quran was taught to me by my grandfather.
When only a child, my grandfather taught me to read the Quran.
My grandfather, when only a child, taught me to read the Quran.
explanation: As written, “when only a child” describes the grandfather; adding “I was” shows that the speaker was the child.

subject: English
q: Choose the sentence that fixes the misplaced or dangling phrase in: “He sold the car to a man with a cracked windscreen.”
o: He sold the car to a man with a cracked windscreen.
With a cracked windscreen, he sold the car to a man.
He, with a cracked windscreen, sold the car to a man.
He sold the car with a cracked windscreen to a man.
explanation: The phrase “with a cracked windscreen” describes the car, so it must be placed next to “the car”.

subject: English
q: The following sentence contains a modifier error: “The waiter served sandwiches to the guests on paper plates.” Choose the correct version.
o: The waiter served sandwiches to the guests on paper plates.
The waiter on paper plates served sandwiches to the guests.
The waiter served the guests sandwiches on paper plates.
On paper plates, the waiter served sandwiches to the guests.
explanation: Placing “on paper plates” immediately after “sandwiches” shows that the sandwiches, not the guests, were on the plates.

subject: English
q: Which sentence corrects the modifier error in: “I bought a horse for my sister that was grey.”?
o: I bought a grey horse for my sister.
I bought a horse for my sister that was grey.
I bought for my sister that was grey a horse.
For my sister that was grey, I bought a horse.
explanation: The description “grey” belongs to the horse; making it an adjective before “horse” removes the confusion.

subject: English
q: Choose the sentence that fixes the misplaced or dangling phrase in: “The professor gave a lecture on pollution in the main hall caused by factories.”
o: Caused by factories, the professor gave a lecture on pollution in the main hall.
In the main hall, the professor gave a lecture on pollution caused by factories.
The professor gave a lecture in the main hall caused by factories on pollution.
The professor gave a lecture on pollution in the main hall caused by factories.
explanation: The phrase “caused by factories” must follow “pollution”, and “in the main hall” should be moved so that it does not split them.

subject: English
q: The following sentence contains a modifier error: “Being late, the doors of the examination hall were closed on him.” Choose the correct version.
o: Being late, closed were the doors of the examination hall on him.
Being late, the doors of the examination hall were closed on him.
The doors of the examination hall, being late, were closed on him.
Because he was late, the doors of the examination hall were closed on him.
explanation: The doors were not late; a clause with its own subject (“because he was late”) corrects the dangling phrase.

subject: English
q: Which sentence corrects the modifier error in: “Reaching the summit, the view was breathtaking.”?
o: The view, reaching the summit, was breathtaking.
When we reached the summit, the view was breathtaking.
Reaching the summit, breathtaking was the view.
Reaching the summit, the view was breathtaking.
explanation: A view cannot reach a summit; a clause with its own subject (“we”) fixes the error.

subject: English
q: Choose the sentence that fixes the misplaced or dangling phrase in: “On entering the room, a strange smell was noticed.”
o: On entering the room, there was noticed a strange smell.
A strange smell, on entering the room, was noticed.
On entering the room, I noticed a strange smell.
On entering the room, a strange smell was noticed.
explanation: The prepositional gerund phrase “on entering the room” needs the person who entered as the subject.

subject: English
q: The following sentence contains a modifier error: “Exhausted after the long match, the bed looked very inviting.” Choose the correct version.
o: Exhausted after the long match, the players found the bed very inviting.
The bed, exhausted after the long match, looked very inviting.
Exhausted after the long match, the bed looked very inviting.
Exhausted after the long match, it was a very inviting bed.
explanation: It was the players, not the bed, who were exhausted, so “the players” must follow the introductory phrase.

subject: English
q: Which sentence corrects the modifier error in: “To apply for a passport, a form must be filled in at the office.”?
o: To apply for a passport, filling in a form at the office is a must.
To apply for a passport, you must fill in a form at the office.
To apply for a passport, a form must be filled in at the office.
A form, to apply for a passport, must be filled in at the office.
explanation: The person applying must be the subject of the main clause; “you” supplies the missing doer.

subject: English
q: Choose the sentence that fixes the misplaced or dangling phrase in: “Walking to the office, a wallet was found on the pavement by Rashid.”
o: A wallet, walking to the office, was found on the pavement by Rashid.
Rashid found a wallet walking to the office on the pavement.
Walking to the office, a wallet was found on the pavement by Rashid.
Walking to the office, Rashid found a wallet on the pavement.
explanation: The person walking (Rashid) must be the subject that immediately follows the participle phrase.

subject: English
q: The following sentence contains a modifier error: “Driving through the Thar desert, several camels were seen by the tourists.” Choose the correct version.
o: Several camels, driving through the Thar desert, were seen by the tourists.
The tourists saw several camels driving through the Thar desert.
Driving through the Thar desert, the tourists saw several camels.
Driving through the Thar desert, several camels were seen by the tourists.
explanation: The tourists, not the camels, were driving, so “the tourists” must be the subject after the phrase; the last option makes the camels seem to drive.

subject: English
q: Which sentence corrects the modifier error in: “In his new uniform, the dog barked at the postman.”?
o: The dog barked at the postman in his new uniform.
In his new uniform, the dog barked at the postman.
The dog barked in his new uniform at the postman.
The dog in his new uniform barked at the postman.
explanation: The phrase “in his new uniform” describes the postman, so it must be placed after “the postman”.

subject: English
q: Choose the sentence that fixes the misplaced or dangling phrase in: “After considering the evidence, the verdict was announced.”
o: After considering the evidence, the verdict was announced.
After considering the evidence, the announcement of the verdict came.
The verdict, after considering the evidence, was announced.
After considering the evidence, the judge announced the verdict.
explanation: The phrase “after considering the evidence” needs a subject that did the considering, i.e. the judge.

subject: English
q: The following sentence contains a modifier error: “There is a letter on the table from my cousin that arrived this morning.” Choose the correct version.
o: A letter that arrived this morning from my cousin is on the table.
From my cousin that arrived this morning, there is a letter on the table.
There is a letter on the table from my cousin that arrived this morning.
There is on the table that arrived this morning a letter from my cousin.
explanation: The clause “that arrived this morning” describes the letter; in the corrected version it sits directly after “letter”.

subject: English
q: Which sentence corrects the modifier error in: “Hoping for a good harvest, the seeds were sown early.”?
o: Hoping for a good harvest, early sowing of the seeds took place.
Hoping for a good harvest, the farmers sowed the seeds early.
Hoping for a good harvest, the seeds were sown early.
The seeds, hoping for a good harvest, were sown early.
explanation: Seeds cannot hope; the farmers must be the subject.

subject: English
q: Choose the sentence that fixes the misplaced or dangling phrase in: “At the age of ten, my grandmother told me stories of Partition.”
o: My grandmother, at the age of ten, told me stories of Partition.
My grandmother told stories of Partition at the age of ten to me.
When I was ten, my grandmother told me stories of Partition.
At the age of ten, my grandmother told me stories of Partition.
explanation: As written, the grandmother seems to be ten; a clause naming the speaker (“when I was ten”) removes the ambiguity.

subject: English
q: The following sentence contains a modifier error: “Using the new software, the report was completed in an hour.” Choose the correct version.
o: Using the new software, the report was completed in an hour.
Using the new software, the analyst completed the report in an hour.
Using the new software, completion of the report took an hour.
The report, using the new software, was completed in an hour.
explanation: A report cannot use software; the analyst must be the subject.

subject: English
q: Which sentence means that Sara, and nobody else, passed the test?
o: Only Sara passed the test.
Sara passed the only test.
Sara only passed the test.
Sara passed only the test.
explanation: “Only” should be placed directly before the word it limits; here it limits “Sara”.

subject: English
q: Which sentence says that the shop opens on Sundays and on no other day?
o: The only shop opens on Sundays.
The shop only opens on Sunday mornings.
Only the shop opens on Sundays.
The shop opens only on Sundays.
explanation: “Only” must stand before “on Sundays” to limit the day.

subject: English
q: Which sentence means that he drank two cups of tea and no more?
o: Only he drank two cups of tea.
He only drank tea from two cups.
He drank only two cups of tea.
He drank two cups of tea only today.
explanation: To limit the quantity, “only” is placed before “two cups”.

subject: English
q: Which sentence says that no one except the minister can sign the order?
o: The minister can only sign the order.
The minister can sign the only order.
The minister can sign only the order.
Only the minister can sign the order.
explanation: “Only” limits the subject when it is placed before “the minister”.

subject: English
q: Which sentence says that he can read English but cannot write or speak it?
o: He can read only English.
Only he can read English.
He can only read English.
He can read English only.
explanation: Placed before the verb “read”, “only” limits the action; the other placements limit the person or the language.

subject: English
q: Which sentence says that English is the one language he can read?
o: He can only read English newspapers.
He can read only English.
He can read English only slowly.
Only he can read English.
explanation: To limit the object, “only” goes directly before “English”.

subject: English
q: Which sentence means that very nearly every student passed?
o: Almost all the students passed.
All the students almost passed.
All the students passed almost.
The students passed almost.
explanation: “Almost” should qualify “all”; “almost passed” would mean they did not quite pass.

subject: English
q: Which sentence says that the storm damaged nearly every house in the village?
o: The storm damaged almost every house in the village.
The storm almost damaged every house in the village.
Almost the storm damaged every house in the village.
The storm damaged every house in the almost village.
explanation: “Almost” must modify “every house”; placed before “damaged”, it would mean no damage actually occurred.

subject: English
q: Which sentence means that the distance walked was a little under ten kilometres?
o: We walked ten nearly kilometres.
Nearly we walked ten kilometres.
We walked nearly ten kilometres.
We nearly walked ten kilometres.
explanation: “Nearly” must qualify the number “ten kilometres”; before “walked” it suggests we almost walked but did not.

subject: English
q: Which sentence says that we reached the station just in time and did catch the train?
o: Nearly the train we missed.
We missed nearly the train.
We missed the nearly train.
We nearly missed the train.
explanation: “Nearly” before the verb means the action almost happened but did not, so we caught the train.

subject: English
q: Which sentence suggests that it is surprising that the teacher could not solve the problem?
o: The teacher could not solve the problem even.
Even the teacher could not solve the problem.
The teacher could not even solve the problem.
The teacher could not solve even the problem.
explanation: “Even” placed before “the teacher” emphasises the surprising subject.

subject: English
q: Which sentence complains that he failed to do so much as thank us?
o: He did not thank even us.
Even he did not thank us.
Even he thanked us.
He did not even thank us.
explanation: “Even” before the verb stresses how little was done: not so much as a word of thanks.

subject: English
q: Which sentence says that the book arrived only two days before the examination?
o: The book just arrived, two days before the examination.
Just the book arrived two days before the examination.
The book arrived just two days before the examination.
The book arrived two days just before examination.
explanation: “Just” qualifies the time phrase “two days before”, meaning “only”.

subject: English
q: Which sentence means that very little food remained?
o: There was any food scarcely left.
There was scarcely any food left.
Scarcely there was any food left.
There scarcely was food left any.
explanation: “Scarcely” modifies “any food”, meaning “almost no food”.

subject: English
q: Which sentence says that the news reached me as recently as yesterday?
o: I heard the news only yesterday.
I heard only the news yesterday.
I only heard the news, yesterday.
Only I heard the news yesterday.
explanation: “Only yesterday” means “as recently as yesterday”; the other placements limit the person, the action or the thing heard.

subject: English
q: Which sentence removes the ambiguity in “People who exercise often live longer”, making clear that frequent exercise is meant?
o: People often who exercise live longer.
People who often exercise live longer.
People who exercise live often longer.
Often people who exercise live longer.
explanation: “Often” between two verbs could modify either; placing it before “exercise” makes it modify the exercising.

subject: English
q: Which sentence makes clear that the doctor quickly told the patient to rest (rather than telling him to rest quickly)?
o: The doctor quickly told the patient to rest.
The doctor told the patient quickly to rest.
The doctor told the patient to rest quickly.
The doctor told the patient to quickly rest.
explanation: Placed before “told”, “quickly” can modify only the telling.

subject: English
q: Which of the following sentences contains a dangling modifier?
o: Because she missed the bus, she reached the office late.
She reached the office late because she had missed the bus.
Having missed the bus, she reached the office late.
Having missed the bus, the office was reached late.
explanation: In the first sentence nothing in the main clause could have missed the bus; the office did not miss it.

subject: English
q: In which sentence is the introductory phrase correctly attached?
o: Tired of waiting, the flight was finally announced.
Tired of waiting, complaints began to be heard.
Tired of waiting, the passengers began to complain.
Tired of waiting, the airport became noisy.
explanation: Only in the first sentence is the subject (“the passengers”) the one who was tired of waiting.

subject: English
q: Which of the following sentences contains a misplaced modifier?
o: She wore a bicycle helmet on her head that was too large.
She wore on her head a bicycle helmet that was too large.
She wore a bicycle helmet that was too large for her.
The bicycle helmet she wore was too large.
explanation: In the first sentence, “that was too large” seems to describe her head rather than the helmet.

subject: English
q: Which sentence corrects the modifier error in: “Flying over Karachi, the sea looked calm and blue.”?
o: The sea, flying over Karachi, looked calm and blue.
Flying over Karachi, the sea looked calm and blue.
Flying over Karachi, we saw that the sea looked calm and blue.
Flying over Karachi, calm and blue the sea looked.
explanation: The sea was not flying; the main clause needs the people on the plane as its subject.

subject: English
q: Choose the sentence that fixes the misplaced or dangling phrase in: “Opening the parcel, several books fell on the floor.”
o: Opening the parcel, on the floor several books fell.
As I opened the parcel, several books fell on the floor.
Opening the parcel, several books fell on the floor.
Several books, opening the parcel, fell on the floor.
explanation: Books cannot open a parcel; a clause with its own subject (“I opened”) removes the dangling participle.

subject: English
q: The following sentence contains a modifier error: “To reduce traffic jams, new flyovers have been built in the city.” Choose the correct version.
o: To reduce traffic jams, new flyovers have been built in the city.
To reduce traffic jams, the building of new flyovers has happened in the city.
New flyovers, to reduce traffic jams, have been built in the city.
To reduce traffic jams, the city government has built new flyovers.
explanation: An introductory purpose phrase should be followed by the agent who has the purpose, here “the city government”.

subject: English
q: Which sentence corrects the modifier error in: “Born in a remote village, education was hard for him to obtain.”?
o: Born in a remote village, education was hard for him to obtain.
Born in a remote village, he found education hard to obtain.
Education, born in a remote village, was hard for him to obtain.
Born in a remote village, it was hard for him to obtain education.
explanation: The participle “born” must attach to the person who was born, so “he” must be the subject.

subject: English
q: Choose the sentence that fixes the misplaced or dangling phrase in: “I read that an earthquake had struck Turkey in the newspaper.”
o: I read in the newspaper that an earthquake had struck Turkey.
I read that an earthquake in the newspaper had struck Turkey.
I read that an earthquake had struck Turkey in the newspaper.
I read that in the newspaper an earthquake had struck Turkey.
explanation: As written, the earthquake seems to have struck Turkey “in the newspaper”; the phrase belongs next to “read”.

subject: English
q: The following sentence contains a modifier error: “She baked a cake for the guests covered with cream.” Choose the correct version.
o: Covered with cream, she baked a cake for the guests.
She, covered with cream, baked a cake for the guests.
She baked a cake for the guests covered with cream.
She baked a cake covered with cream for the guests.
explanation: The phrase “covered with cream” describes the cake and must be placed directly after it.

subject: English
q: Which sentence corrects the modifier error in: “Turning the corner, the museum came into view.”?
o: The museum, turning the corner, came into view.
Turning the corner, the museum came into view.
Turning the corner, we saw the museum come into view.
Turning the corner, into view the museum came.
explanation: A museum cannot turn a corner; the people turning it must be the subject.

subject: English
q: Choose the sentence that fixes the misplaced or dangling phrase in: “As a young student, the library was my second home.”
o: As a young student, my second home was the library.
As a young student, I treated the library as my second home.
The library, as a young student, was my second home.
As a young student, the library was my second home.
explanation: The phrase “as a young student” must describe the subject; the library was not a student, so “I” must be the subject.

subject: English
q: The following sentence contains a modifier error: “For sale: a piano by a lady with carved wooden legs.” Choose the correct version.
o: For sale: a piano owned by a lady with carved wooden legs.
For sale: a piano by a lady with carved wooden legs.
For sale: by a lady with carved wooden legs, a piano.
For sale: a piano with carved wooden legs, offered by a lady.
explanation: The phrase “with carved wooden legs” describes the piano, so it must follow “piano”, not “lady”.

subject: English
q: Which sentence corrects the modifier error in: “After waiting for three hours, the doctor finally saw us.”?
o: The doctor, after waiting for three hours, finally saw us.
After waiting for three hours, the doctor was finally seen by us.
After we had waited for three hours, the doctor finally saw us.
After waiting for three hours, the doctor finally saw us.
explanation: The phrase “after waiting” refers to the patients, not the doctor; giving it its own subject (“we had waited”) fixes it.

subject: English
q: Choose the sentence that fixes the misplaced or dangling phrase in: “While studying abroad, his father passed away.”
o: While he was studying abroad, his father passed away.
His father, while studying abroad, passed away.
While studying abroad, his father’s death occurred.
While studying abroad, his father passed away.
explanation: As written, the father seems to have been studying abroad; a clause with its own subject (“he was”) makes the meaning clear.

subject: English
q: The following sentence contains a modifier error: “The old man walked his dog in a woollen coat.” Choose the correct version.
o: The old man walked his dog, which was in a woollen coat.
In a woollen coat, the old man walked his dog.
The old man walked his dog in a woollen coat.
His dog, in a woollen coat, was walked by the old man.
explanation: Moving “in a woollen coat” next to “the old man” shows that he, not the dog, was wearing the coat.

subject: English
q: Which sentence corrects the modifier error in: “Having studied hard, the examination seemed easy.”?
o: The examination, having studied hard, seemed easy.
Having studied hard, the examination seemed easy.
Having studied hard, Nadia found the examination easy.
Having studied hard, easy the examination seemed.
explanation: The person who studied, Nadia, must be the subject after the participle phrase.

subject: English
q: Which sentence says that Asad has no brothers or sisters?
o: Asad only is a child.
Asad is only a child.
Only Asad is a child.
Asad is an only child.
explanation: “An only child” means a child with no siblings; “only a child” means “merely a child”.

subject: English
q: Which sentence excuses Bilal’s mistake on the ground that he is very young?
o: Bilal is only a child.
Bilal is an only child.
Only Bilal is a child.
Bilal only is the child.
explanation: “Only a child” means “merely a child”, which excuses the mistake because of his age.

subject: English
q: Which sentence says that there were only a few pages left for her to read?
o: She has finished the almost book.
Almost she has finished the book.
She has almost finished the book.
She has finished almost the book.
explanation: “Almost” before the main verb “finished” means she is close to finishing.

subject: English
q: Which sentence stresses that he works every day, including Sundays?
o: He works on even Sundays.
He even works, on Sundays.
Even he works on Sundays.
He works even on Sundays.
explanation: “Even” before “on Sundays” emphasises the surprising time.

subject: English
q: Which sentence means that very few people came to the meeting?
o: Hardly came anyone to the meeting.
Hardly anyone came to the meeting.
Anyone hardly came to the meeting.
Anyone came hardly to the meeting.
explanation: “Hardly anyone” means “almost no one”.
